Technical Writing Portfolio · Scott Harmer · 2026

This case study documents my review and rework of an audio-visual annotation information product within an AI data workflow. As the Information Product Reviewer, I assessed the product against established methodology guidelines and determined where targeted editing was sufficient and where structural rework was required.

The reworked product progressed from 3 broad tracks and 31 data entries to 11 specific tracks and 35 data entries. It subsequently passed to randomised quality control with only one edge-case terminology adjustment and no further structural rebuild required.

section.title: What This Case Study Demonstrates
section.p: Requirements and feedback analysis · editorial judgement · information architecture · taxonomy design · metadata writing · classification design · quality assurance · complex-content restructuring

body.p: As an Information Product Reviewer, I assessed and reworked an audio annotation information product produced by a subject matter expert (SME). The product used metadata labels and corresponding metadata descriptions to define tracks, with individual sound data entries assigned to each track. Following my review and rework, the information product comprised 11 specific tracks containing 35 data entries.

The initial product used three broad tracks: Background Music, Human Sounds, and Sound Effects. My review identified significant issues with specificity, consistency, terminology, visual descriptions, data classification, and the relationship between individual entries and their assigned tracks. Using the established methodology guidelines as my reference, I refined the metadata labels and descriptions, standardised descriptive language, corrected data-entry classifications, and restructured the tracks to create a more precise and consistently organised information product.

Producing a high-quality audio annotation information product involves two distinct layers of information: the individual data entries and the metadata that organises them into tracks. Each has its own requirements, making it essential to maintain a clear separation between what describes an individual sound and what defines its broader classification.

At the data-entry level, each annotation must describe a sound accurately and consistently, using language based only on what can be identified through audio. At the metadata level, labels and descriptions must be specific enough to distinguish meaningful sound categories, while entries must be correctly grouped so that their relationship to the assigned track remains accurate and clear.

A further challenge is maintaining the boundary between audio and visual information. Visual details belong in their designated metadata field and must remain separate from metadata descriptions and data entries intended to describe sound.

The initial information product did not meet the required quality standards across these areas. Addressing the issues therefore required a methodical, guideline-based review of the metadata structure, descriptive language, data-entry classification, and the relationships between individual entries and their assigned tracks.

p.xref: ↑ Back to Case Study at a Glance

body.p: The information product supported a downstream AI/ML data workflow, where structured audio annotations could be used as training or evaluation data. This made consistency, specificity, and reliable classification especially important, as the information needed to be interpretable both by human reviewers and by the systems processing the structured data.
The immediate human audience also included subject matter experts and reviewers responsible for producing, evaluating, and maintaining the quality of the annotated information.

I work as an Information Product Reviewer at the third stage of the production workflow, following two subject matter expert (SME) stages. My responsibility is to assess each information product against the established methodology guidelines and determine the level of intervention required before it progresses toward client delivery.

Depending on the quality of the product, I either make targeted edits to resolve specific issues or carry out a complete rebuild when the structure, classification, or descriptive content does not meet the required standard. My review covers metadata, data-entry descriptions, taxonomy, classification, consistency, and the separation of information types.

After my review, the information product passes through one final internal stage before delivery to the client. I have maintained a personal compliance grade of 4.6/5, compared with a team average of 4.3/5.

p.xref: ↑ Back to Case Study at a Glance

body.p: Rather than making isolated wording changes, I treated the evaluation findings as interconnected issues within the information structure.

I first separated the evaluation feedback into three distinct problem areas. This allowed me to identify recurring issues across the information product and establish a structured basis for the review.

strow.stentry: Metadata labels; metadata descriptions; level of specificity; separation of information types
Descriptive language; consistency; ambiguity; language use; classification and grouping

body.p: Categorising the feedback in this way helped me address recurring issues systematically rather than treating each correction as an isolated problem.

The original three-track structure was too broad to represent the different sound types with sufficient specificity. As part of my review, I reworked the taxonomy by separating broad categories into more precise tracks, using the guidelines to determine how distinct sound types should be classified.
The taxonomy expanded from 3 broad tracks to 11 specific tracks:

The metadata descriptions were revised to provide more specific, identifiable characteristics for each track. I reviewed the descriptions against the methodology guidelines and refined them to distinguish relevant qualities such as pitch, frequency, sound quality, vocal characteristics, language, and mechanical or electronic properties.
This made the metadata more informative and helped define the characteristics that distinguished one track from another.

strow.stentry: Woman speaking English in a medium-pitched voice.
Man speaking in a medium-pitched voice in a non-English language.

body.p: Together, these revisions created clearer distinctions between tracks and provided a more consistent metadata structure for classifying individual data entries.

Each track is defined by its metadata label and metadata description, with individual data entries assigned according to their sound characteristics. During the review, I identified issues with classification and grouping, including entries that did not align clearly with their assigned tracks.

I reviewed these relationships against the guidelines and reclassified entries where necessary, creating a clearer and more consistent connection between the individual sound descriptions and the tracks used to organise them.

image.alt: Track 4, Deep Breathing, linked to assigned data entries.

body.p: This structure creates a clear relationship between each track’s metadata and the individual data entries assigned to it, making classifications easier to interpret, review, and validate.

I reviewed the individual data-entry descriptions for consistency, specificity, and adherence to the guidelines. The initial entries contained ambiguous or inconsistent language, mixed information types, and descriptions that did not always represent the sound precisely.

I standardised the descriptions using identifiable audio characteristics such as frequency, pitch, duration, repetition, intensity, sound quality, and vocal or mechanical properties. This created a more consistent descriptive pattern across the information product while preserving the characteristics of each individual sound.

strow.stentry: #1 A creepy background music from an offscreen source featuring sustained dissonant harmonies and percussion sounds.
#1 Eerie electronic music with rhythmic percussive beats, heavy thuds, faint bells, and haunting wailing.
#5 A man calling a non-English name.
#5 Medium-pitched male speech in a non-English language.
#6 Two rapid, shallow exhales of breath.

body.p: Standardising the descriptive language improved consistency across the data-entry layer and made individual sounds easier to interpret, classify, and review against the methodology guidelines.

The review identified cases where visual information had been included in fields intended to describe audio. To maintain a clear separation between information types, I removed visual references from metadata descriptions and individual audio data entries and kept visual details within their designated field.
This ensured that each field served a distinct purpose: audio descriptions documented identifiable sound characteristics, while visual information remained separate within the metadata structure.
Separating information by type improved clarity, reduced ambiguity, and helped maintain a more consistent information structure across the product.

body.p: The review resulted in a fully reworked audio annotation information product, with changes spanning the taxonomy, metadata, data-entry descriptions, classification structure, and separation of information types.

strow.stentry: Final structure comprising 11 tracks and 35 data entries.
Reworked from 3 broad tracks to 11 specific sound categories.
More specific metadata labels and descriptions defining each track.
A reworked set of 35 audio descriptions using more consistent and identifiable sound characteristics.
Data entries reassigned and grouped according to their appropriate tracks, supported by the final correlation legend.
Audio and visual information kept within their designated fields.

body.p: Following the rework, the information product met the required methodology standards to progress to the next quality-control stage. During randomised QC, only one edge-case terminology adjustment was made: “apparition” was changed to “haunting” in the Track 8 metadata description, while “apparition” was retained in the designated visual description field. This preserved the distinction between audio and visual information while aligning the metadata terminology with the applicable guideline standard.

The technical complexity of the project came from understanding how multiple layers of structured information interacted within a guideline-driven annotation system. Effective review required more than editing individual descriptions; I needed to understand the information model, classification logic, terminology rules, and relationships between metadata, tracks, data entries, and visual information.

strow.stentry: Metadata label + metadata description define a track, with individual data entries assigned to that track.
Distinct sound characteristics had to be identified and organised into sufficiently specific categories while maintaining accurate entry-to-track relationships.
Audio and visual information followed different requirements and needed to remain within their designated fields.
Each decision had to align with established methodology guidelines, including terminology, specificity, classification, and edge-case usage.

body.p: Working within these constraints required me to evaluate each change at both the individual-entry level and the wider information-structure level, ensuring that local edits remained consistent with the product as a whole.

The rework produced a more granular, consistent, and clearly organised information product that met the required methodology standard to progress to quality control. The final structure comprised 11 specific tracks and 35 data entries, with clearer metadata definitions, more precise classification, and standardised descriptive language.

Overall, the rework improved the product’s structure, consistency, and classification accuracy while reducing the need for further intervention at the QC stage. The outcome demonstrates the value of applying technical-writing principles beyond sentence-level editing, particularly through clearer terminology, stronger classification, consistent descriptions, and more effective taxonomy, metadata, and information architecture.

p.xref: ↑ Back to Case Study at a Glance

body.p: This project reinforced that effective technical writing extends beyond improving individual sentences. In a structured information product, clarity depends on how taxonomy, metadata, classification, descriptive language, and information boundaries work together.

It also strengthened my judgement in deciding when targeted editing is sufficient and when a product requires a more substantial rebuild. Reviewing both individual entries and the wider information structure helped me make changes that were accurate at the local level while remaining consistent across the product.
The QC outcome also highlighted the importance of precise terminology in edge cases, particularly when a term may be appropriate in one information field but not another.
This project combined structured content review, technical editing, information architecture, and quality assurance within a guideline-driven AI data workflow.
Core competencies: Information architecture · Taxonomy · Metadata · Technical editing · Content review · Quality assurance · Guideline compliance
